# Selection — TRD §15 row 11: which device-to-device ceremony

**Status:** selected, and folded into the TRD. **Date:** 2026-08-19
**Closes:** TRD §15 row 11 · **Scope of:** review 3b (protocol)
**Constrained by:** TRD §13.6, §13.4, §13.2, §10.11, §12 · PRD §7.6 · **Stage:** [sequencing.md](../sequencing.md) §3.5
**Vectors:** [`test/vectors/enrollment-ceremony.json`](../../test/vectors/enrollment-ceremony.json), generated by
[`scripts/generate-enrollment-vectors.mjs`](../../scripts/generate-enrollment-vectors.mjs)
**Companions:** [row 14](./row-14-recovery-code.md) supplies the alphabet, the mask and the normalization, reused
whole; [row 13](./row-13-device-lock.md) established the rule this row applies to cameras;
[row 5](./row-5-finalization.md) is the other half of what a hostile service must not be able to do.
**Amended by:** [row 9](./row-9-chain-head-discovery.md) — the transcript binds the epoch head, so the typed
symbols authenticate where the lineage is as well as whose key it is. The short string changed with it.
**Amended by:** [`S0-2`](../review/remediation/S0-2/README.md) (2026-08-27) — a successful ceremony now **produces a certified recipient-set successor** (TRD §§13.5–13.6), and
the transcript binds the recovery recipient as well as the wrapping key. The ceremony was sound for the immediate
release and silent about the delayed one; that is what this amendment repairs.
**Amended by:** [`S0-2`](../review/remediation/S0-2/README.md) (2026-08-28, the return) — the transcript binds the new device's **signing** public key, because the
member entry the successor certifies is now `(credential_id ‖ W_pub ‖ S_pub)` and an approval verifies under
member `S_pub`s (`P-1`, ratified): the SAS vouches for the signing key as well as the wrapping key. The vector
file republishes with **every transcript input in the published inputs** — `FU-05` found `recovery_state_digest`
inserted by generator internals and absent from the formula and inputs, so the artifact could not be
independently reconstructed; `pnpm recipient:check` now reconstructs it from the published inputs alone.
**Amended 2026-09-16:** the operator selected restart on a competing epoch change rather than
automatic sibling rebasing. See §7 and [the content-approval plan](../account-content-approval-prep.md).
The selected primitive bytes and published vectors are unchanged.

---

## The selection

```
A short authentication string over an in-band agreement, committed before it is
revealed, and typed rather than compared. QR is an accelerator of the same
transcript where the platform supplies a decoder, never a second protocol.

Commit                  before either nonce is revealed

  n_E, n_N   32 bytes each from crypto.getRandomValues()
  c_r = SHA-256( LP("done/enroll-commit/v1") || LP(role) || LP(hex n_r) )
        role in { "existing", "new" }

The transcript

  T = LP("done/enroll/v1") || LP(workspace_id) || LP(dec epoch)
      || LP(hex epoch_head)
      || LP(existing_credential_id) || LP(new_credential_id)
      || LP(hex W_pub) || LP(hex S_pub) || LP(hex recovery_state_digest)
      || LP(hex n_E) || LP(hex n_N)

  W_pub  the new device's X25519 wrapping public key (§13.4) — the value this
         whole ceremony exists to authenticate.
  S_pub  the new device's Ed25519 signing public key (S0-2 return, P-1
         ratified). The successor's member entry is
         (credential_id ‖ W_pub ‖ S_pub) and set approvals verify under member
         S_pub's, so the one place a person vouches for a key must vouch for
         this one too — or the service substitutes it in the entry the honest
         existing device certifies and holds the approval authority the set
         exists to withhold from it.
  recovery_state_digest
         the recovery recipient the new device will install (TRD §13.5). Bound
         here because substituting R_pub is this row's attack at a second
         carrier: a service that hands the new device an attacker-controlled
         R_pub and a matching opaque envelope gets the HONEST new device to
         wrap future generations to it. The existing device cannot be induced
         to certify a recovery recipient it does not itself hold.
  th     = SHA-256(T), the ceremony's identity.

On success              the existing device signs a CERTIFIED RECIPIENT-SET
                        SUCCESSOR (TRD §§13.5-13.6) naming (new_credential_id,
                        W_pub, S_pub) and this recovery state; the new
                        credential countersigns on install. That record, not
                        the epoch roster, is what a future rotator reads.

                        This ceremony was sound for the IMMEDIATE release and
                        silent about the delayed one. Without the successor,
                        an unrelated rotation later wraps K_(g+1) to every
                        credential in a service-signed roster -- which is
                        authorization causing key delivery after all.

The string

  SAS = HKDF-SHA256(ikm = T, salt = "", info = LP("done/enroll-sas/v1"), L = 5)
        symbol i = ALPHABET[byte_i & 0x1f]        e.g. R76MR

  Alphabet, mask and normalization are row 14's, unchanged: Crockford Base32
  without I, L, O, U; 256 = 8 x 32 so the mask is uniform; O -> 0, I -> 1,
  L -> 1 on input, U rejected.
  Five symbols, 25 bits. One guess per admitted credential — not per attempt.

Direction               displayed on the NEW device, typed into the EXISTING one

The wrap                HPKE base to W_pub (row 1)
  info = LP("done/enroll-wrap/v1") || LP(hex th)
  So a wrap made for this ceremony opens under no other.

On mismatch             the enrollment is refused and the credential is spent.
                        Re-enrolling mints a new credential and a new transcript.
                        There is no retry of the same ceremony.

                LP(s) = uint16be(byteLength(utf8 s)) || utf8 s
```

Everything below is why, and what it cost.

---

## 1. What is actually being authenticated, which is narrower than "the device"

§13.6's second gate is one sentence: **service authorization alone must never cause an existing client to
release a content key.** Unpacked, that means the existing device must learn the new device's **wrapping public
key** through a channel the service does not control. Not its identity, not its name, not that a human is
present — one 32-byte value, learned authentically.

That narrowing does the work. Both of the ceremonies §15 named before the fold are ways to carry one public key
across a channel a hostile service cannot forge, and they differ only in **whether a machine or a person
carries it**:

| The candidate §15 listed    | The out-of-band channel is |
| --------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| QR carrying the key         | A camera reading a screen  |
| Short authentication string | A person reading a screen  |

Neither removes the out-of-band channel. **There is no construction that does**, and §11.2 test 7 is the test
that would catch anyone who thought otherwise: a malicious service presenting a valid successor epoch must be
refused, and only something outside the service's control can refuse it.

---

## 2. QR is not the root, and the reason is row 13's, applied to cameras

The camera path is attractive: no human comparison step, no transcription, and the natural physical arrangement
(a phone held in front of a laptop) is exactly the enrollment case. It is still declined as the **root**, on
three grounds that compound.

**A decoder does not fit the bundle.** Reading a QR code needs a decoder, and encoding one does not.
`BarcodeDetector` is native in Chrome and Edge and on Android; **it is in neither Safari nor Firefox**, so a
product that depends on it must ship a JavaScript decoder as well. [performance.md](../performance.md) records
**43.7 kB of gzipped headroom** against §12's 350 kB budget, and **row 2's WASM candidate for the measured
journal breach wants 24.3 kB of it.** A decoder would be competing for that headroom with a fix for a defect
that is already measured. That is not a close call.

**Availability is a matrix, not a version.** Row 13 closed its open question with the finding that WebAuthn
PRF's availability "is a matrix of OS, browser and authenticator kind rather than a version", and concluded that
**a capability that ragged cannot be a root.** Camera access is the same shape and then some: browser support
for the decoder, an OS permission prompt, a physical camera on the existing device, a lens that can focus at
laptop-to-phone distance, and adequate light. §10.11's Baseline floor has nothing to say about most of that.

**And the direction is wrong for the security decision.** The device that must be convinced is the **existing**
one, since it is the one releasing a content key. A new-device-displays / existing-device-scans flow therefore
needs the camera on the laptop — the device least likely to have a usable one pointed in the right direction.

**So the rule row 13 established is applied a third time**: the ragged capability becomes an accelerator of the
selected construction rather than a branch in it. Where `BarcodeDetector` exists, the new device may render the
SAS's transcript as a QR code and the existing device may read it instead of the person typing. **Same
transcript, same 25 bits, same failure mode** — the security argument does not fork, and there is no
device-dependent security bar. §13.8's sentence covers this too: optionality is not a product branch.

---

## 3. Typed, not compared — and this is a real decision, not presentation

The conventional SAS flow shows the string on both devices and asks the person to confirm they match.
**A confirmation is satisfied by pressing the affirmative button**, which is what a person does when they are
enrolling their own phone and have no expectation of an attack. The step that is meant to be the entire security
boundary is the step most likely to be discharged without being performed.

**Transcription is not skippable in the same way.** The person cannot type `R76MR` into the laptop without
having read `R76MR` off the phone. The check moves from _did you compare_ to _can you produce_, and only the
second is evidence.

**It costs one input field that already exists.** Row 14 built the recovery-code input: Crockford Base32,
five-symbol grouping, and a normalization that folds `O` to `0` and `I`/`L` to `1` so a correct transcription of
a badly rendered code still works. **This is that field at one group instead of five.** Reusing it means one
alphabet in the product, one normalization, one set of confusable-character rules, and one uniformity proof —
rather than a second short-code format invented three months later that happens to include `O`.

**The honest limit, since it is a human gate.** A person who types five characters from a screen an attacker
controls is not protected, and nothing here changes that. What this buys is that **the attacker must control the
screen**, which is a different and much larger capability than controlling the service — and controlling the
service is precisely the threat §13.6's second gate names.

---

## 4. Twenty-five bits, and why the commitment is what makes them mean anything

**The strength is per admitted credential, not per attempt**, and that is the whole argument for the number.

A service substituting its own wrapping key gets one ceremony per credential it can get admitted. A mismatch
does not offer a retry: **the enrollment is refused and the credential is spent**, so a second attempt is a
second admitted credential and a second visible enrollment failure in front of the person who just watched the
first one fail. §11.2 test 11 already requires interrupted enrollment to fail closed; this row adds that
_closed_ means the credential does not get another turn.

So 25 bits is 1 in 33.5 million per admitted credential, with each failure alarming. Six symbols would be 30
bits and one more character to type; the marginal buyer is small against an attack that is loud at the first
failure.

**None of which is true without the commitment, and the vectors demonstrate it rather than assert it.**
Whichever side reveals its nonce second can search that nonce until the SAS comes out however it likes, because
the SAS is a deterministic function of a transcript that side is still choosing. The generator does exactly
that, with the substituted wrapping key in place, and searches for the first two symbols of the honest
ceremony's string:

> **Target `R7`, found in 401 tries.**

Ten bits, so the count is what probability predicts, and the search is deterministic — candidate _i_ is
`SHA-256("done/grind-demo" || i)` — so that number is a fact about the construction rather than about the
machine that ran it. **Forcing all five symbols is the same search at 2²⁵**, which is seconds. Commit-reveal is
therefore not ceremony around the ceremony; without it the SAS carries zero bits against a service that speaks
second, and _zero_ is the correct figure rather than a rhetorical one.

**`role` is bound inside the commitment** for row 3's stated reason — a binding that costs nothing and removes a
class of confusion is taken. Without it the two commitments are structurally identical and one side's can be
echoed back as the other's.

---

## 5. The wrap is bound to the ceremony, or the ceremony authenticates nothing

The most available way to get this wrong is to treat the ceremony and the delivery as two steps: authenticate
`W_pub`, then wrap `K_g` to it. **A service that can choose which wrap is delivered can then authenticate
ceremony A and hand over the wrap from ceremony B**, and every check above still passes.

The `info` closes it. HPKE base mode binds `info` into the key schedule, so a wrap sealed with
`LP("done/enroll-wrap/v1") || LP(hex th)` **opens only under that transcript hash** — the one containing the
`W_pub` the person authenticated, the epoch it happened at, and both credential ids. A wrap from another
ceremony is not a wrong wrap that gets rejected; it is bytes that do not decrypt.

**This is where the row leans on row 1 and stops.** The HPKE seal itself is row 1's primitive (base mode,
DHKEM(X25519, HKDF-SHA256) / HKDF-SHA256 / AES-256-GCM) and row 4's framing. What is selected here is the
`info`, because it is the only part of the wrap that this ceremony determines.

---

## 6. What it costs

| Cost                | Size                                                                                                                    |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Bundle              | **Nothing.** SHA-256, HKDF and X25519 are WebCrypto (row 1); the alphabet and normalization are row 14's, already built |
| Round trips         | Two, and they are inherent: commitments must both be in before either nonce is out                                      |
| The person          | Five characters, once per device, at a moment they are already setting up a device                                      |
| Both devices online | Yes, and this is the one real cost — see below                                                                          |

**Enrollment requires both devices awake, and rotation deliberately does not.** §13.7 is explicit that rotation
is store-and-forward — "not both-devices-awake" — because a remaining reader must get a new key without the
rotating device waiting for it. **Enrollment is the opposite and has to be**, since the out-of-band channel is a
person looking at two screens. Worth stating so the asymmetry is a decision rather than an inconsistency
somebody finds later: **the interactive requirement is the price of §13.6's second gate, and the escape hatch
already exists** — §13.6 offers "or unwraps it with an independent recovery factor", which is the recovery code
and needs no second device at all.

---

## 7. What Stage 4 owes, and what is not in this row

**The failure copy is the part most likely to come back changed from 3b**, and it is not written here. A SAS
mismatch is either a mistyped character or an attack on a content key, the product cannot tell which, and the
two need the same screen. Row 13 has the same shape and resolved it by requiring **two texts rather than one**
because the consequence has two sizes; this needs the reverse — one text that is honest without being alarming
about the overwhelmingly likely case. That is a product question with a security constraint, and it belongs in
front of the reviewer as a question.

**Two smaller obligations.** The credential must be spent on mismatch, which means the refusal path has to reach
the authorization service and not merely close a dialog. The existing device must also retain the terminal
decision under its own authenticated custody: the service alone cannot keep the budget against a hostile
service. And the transcript binds `epoch` and its head, so a **competing** successor requires fresh
credential/admission, transcript and code entry. Exact resumption preserves the old transcript and decision;
the ceremony's own exact, verified certification successor completes it. Never rebase a prior typed approval.

**Restart cannot undo release.** If a wrapped key has already left the existing device, keep its immutable
pending-certificate/delivery record and do not certify it at another parent. The candidate may possess the
key but remains uncertified; removing future access is rotation, not restarting a dialog. The first private
admission runtime supports one child only, so automatic replacement admission is a separate dependency.
Until implemented, report restart-required rather than recycle a credential. These rulings supersede TRD
§13.6's former automatic sibling-rebuild paragraph and leave the historical vectors unchanged.

**Not in this row.** Admitting the new credential and signing the successor epoch is §13.6's **first** gate, and
rows 9 and 12. The HPKE seal is row 1's primitive and row 4's framing. What a brand-new device does to find the
current chain head before any of this is row 9. Enrollment's effect on the accepted chain — the new credential
starting at the empty chain — is [row 5](./row-5-finalization.md).

---

## 8. The vectors

`node scripts/generate-enrollment-vectors.mjs` writes them; `--check` fails if they are stale, and `pnpm check`
now runs it with the other ten.

**One honest ceremony and fifteen negatives.** A laptop enrolling a phone at epoch 9, with both commitments, the
transcript, its hash, the wrap `info` and the short string. Then every bound field of both constructions, one
at a time — `substituted-signing-key` joined at the `S0-2` return, when the transcript gained `S_pub`.

**`substituted-wrapping-key` is §11.2 test 7 as a value.** The keypairs are RFC 7748 §6.1's — Alice is the new
device, Bob is the key the service offers in her place — and the generator derives each public key from its own
scalar and refuses to write the file unless they match, which is row 14's rule.

**`stale-epoch-head` arrived with [row 9](./row-9-chain-head-discovery.md), one commit after this row was
selected.** The transcript gained the epoch head beside the epoch number, because a device enrolling here is
talking to one that already knows where the lineage is — so the five symbols disagree when a service feeds the
new device a stale head, and row 9 never has to reach this arrival path. **Nothing had been built, so the
amendment cost a regenerated vector file and a changed short string.** After the first deployment it would have
cost a protocol version, which is the general case [sequencing.md](../sequencing.md) §2.1 is about.

**`transposed-nonces` is the one that is not obvious.** Exchanging `n_E` and `n_N` must produce a different
string, because otherwise the transcript is a set rather than a sequence and the ceremony has no roles. Fixed
positions under length prefixes give that; the negative is what proves it, and it is the kind of property that
survives a rewrite only if something is watching.

**Every field is isolated, and here that claim is exact.** `pnpm vectors:coverage` elides each bound field in
turn and confirms exactly one negative stops failing — 14 fields across the two constructions.
Unlike [row 5](./row-5-finalization.md), which has two layers and therefore a field that rescues
every negative in the layer below it, **this construction is flat**: the SAS is a function of the transcript and
nothing else, so a per-field negative isolates a per-field binding and the `aad-only-` naming means what it
says.

**Two things are inputs here that are not inputs in production**, said in the file's own text so a reader who
arrives at the JSON without this document cannot confuse them: the nonces are fixed, because a vector has to fix
one to be a vector — **and the fixing is not the discipline, the commitment is** — and the grinding
demonstration is not production code, it is the reason the commit phase exists.
